description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the "Miasma" / "Phantom Gyp" npm
supply-chain worm (StepSecurity + Snyk disclosure, 2026-06-03; a
descendant of the Shai-Hulud worm family, distinct from the earlier
Mini Shai-Hulud / Nx campaign cluster already in this corpus). Compromised
57 npm packages across 286+ malicious versions in a rolling campaign
under two hours, first observed via `@vapi-ai/server-sdk` (408,000+
monthly downloads).

Attack mechanism ("Phantom Gyp"): a 157-byte `binding.gyp` file abuses
node-gyp's `<!(...)` command-substitution syntax to run an arbitrary
shell command during the gyp CONFIGURE phase, before any compiler runs --
`"sources": ["<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)"]` with
`"type": "none"` (nothing is actually compiled; the command's side effect
is the point). npm auto-invokes `node-gyp rebuild` whenever it sees a
`binding.gyp` file, and this happens WITHOUT declaring any
preinstall/postinstall lifecycle script in `package.json` -- invisible to
tooling that only watches install-hook fields. The `index.js` payload
that runs is a 4.5MB obfuscated loader (ROT-14, then AES-128-GCM
self-decryption) that downloads and executes a Bun runtime binary
(`bun-v1.3.13`) to run the actual 649KB credential-stealer payload under
Bun instead of Node -- process-tree monitoring that only watches for
`node.exe` child processes never sees the credential-theft stage.

Detection logic (CORRELATION, revised 2026-09-04 -- see this corpus's
rule-defects report): the ORIGINAL single-event `and` condition combining
a gyp-rebuild step and a Bun-runtime fetch/exec could never fire, since
the two are separate process-creation events that never share one log

description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the ClawHavoc Claude Code Skills
malicious skill cluster (Docker AI Coding Agent Horror Stories Issue 1 anchor,
May 2026; 335+ malicious skills observed across the public Claude Code skills
ecosystem). Fourth vector of the Nx campaign supply-chain cluster (related
vectors in this corpus: Mini Shai-Hulud npm + s1ngularity Nx CLI +
nx-console VS Code extension). Attack chain:

(1) Attacker publishes a malicious Claude Code skill (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`)
to a public skills ecosystem (npm-style index OR direct curl install snippet
in a blog post / Stack Overflow answer / AI-coding tutorial).
(2) Victim developer installs the skill into their workspace under
`.claude/skills/<malicious-name>/`. Skill content includes a `SKILL.md` with
high-coverage description that surfaces aggressively for many common prompts.
(3) Claude Code surfaces the malicious skill on a routine prompt. The skill
declares broad tool access (Read + Write + Bash + Edit) and executes its
payload during routine workflow.
(4) Payload sweeps credential locations (`.aws/credentials`, `.npmrc`,
`.ssh/`, GitHub tokens, environment variables, 1Password vault, kubeconfig),
bulk-exfils over HTTPS POST to attacker infrastructure, optionally pivots to
other tools (npm install of secondary stage). Some variants hide their
presence via T1564 (Hide Artifacts) by renaming themselves or backdating
filesystem timestamps.

Detection logic (CORRELATION, revised 2026-09-04 -- see this corpus's
rule-defects report): the ORIGINAL single-event condition (install-touchpoint
AND (credential-scan OR bulk-egress OR hide-artifacts)) could never fire
against the actual attack chain as narrated above -- the skill-install
touchpoint and the post-install payload activity are separate
process-creation events, AND the two selections' own `ParentImage` sets did
not even overlap on the credential-scan branch (`claude.exe`/`cursor.exe`
vs. `node.exe`/`powershell.exe`), making that branch structurally
unreachable regardless of event timing. This rule now expresses the two
stages as a `temporal_ordered` correlation: a Claude Code/Cursor-attributed
skill-install/egress touchpoint, FOLLOWED BY a post-install process either
touching a credential location, bulk-egressing, or hiding its own artifacts,
on the same host within a short window.

Related rules (Nx campaign cluster; a fifth vector, Megalodon, was added
later -- see that rule's note on its sourcing): cross-reference
observed_mini_shai_hulud_npm_supply_chain_c2_t1071.yml (1st vector) +
observed_s1ngularity_nx_npm_token_exfil_t1195_002.yml (2nd vector) +
observed_nx_console_t1195_002.yml (3rd vector) in the same corpus.

Source: first-party Docker engineering blog post (docker.com/blog/
ai-coding-agent-horror-stories-security-risks 2026-05). Aggregated from
1 first-party Docker disclosure (Issue 1 of 5-issue serial roadmap).
falsepositives: Legitimate developer install of a public skill into `.claude/skills/` with broad tool permissions for a personal workflow (review skill provenance + publisher reputation; pin known-safe skill source) -- exclude known-trusted publisher identities

AI coding assistant tutorials / educational content that demonstrate skill install + credential reading (e.g., legitimate `aws sts get-caller-identity` example) -- exclude by tutorial-marker comment in SKILL.md
Build pipeline that legitimately reads `.npmrc` / `GITHUB_TOKEN` as part of CI workflow (exclude by source-host CI runner hostname or session-user svc-account)

The `Computer`-level group-by correlates same-host activity, not same-process-tree activity -- a developer machine running many concurrent, unrelated Claude Code sessions and credential-adjacent tooling could coincidentally satisfy the ordering within the 5-minute window; narrow further with a process-tree/session correlation field if your log source provides one
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment; Claude Code product attribution and skill execution surface require environment-specific log source tuning

description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the ClawHavoc Claude Code Skills
malicious skill cluster (Docker AI Coding Agent Horror Stories Issue 1 anchor,
May 2026; 335+ malicious skills observed across the public Claude Code skills
ecosystem). Fourth vector of the Nx campaign supply-chain cluster (related
vectors in this corpus: Mini Shai-Hulud npm + s1ngularity Nx CLI +
nx-console VS Code extension). Attack chain:

(1) Attacker publishes a malicious Claude Code skill (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`)
to a public skills ecosystem (npm-style index OR direct curl install snippet
in a blog post / Stack Overflow answer / AI-coding tutorial).
(2) Victim developer installs the skill into their workspace under
`.claude/skills/<malicious-name>/`. Skill content includes a `SKILL.md` with
high-coverage description that surfaces aggressively for many common prompts.
(3) Claude Code surfaces the malicious skill on a routine prompt. The skill
declares broad tool access (Read + Write + Bash + Edit) and executes its
payload during routine workflow.
(4) Payload sweeps credential locations (`.aws/credentials`, `.npmrc`,
`.ssh/`, GitHub tokens, environment variables, 1Password vault, kubeconfig),
bulk-exfils over HTTPS POST to attacker infrastructure, optionally pivots to
other tools (npm install of secondary stage). Some variants hide their
presence via T1564 (Hide Artifacts) by renaming themselves or backdating
filesystem timestamps.

Detection logic (CORRELATION, revised 2026-09-04 -- see this corpus's
rule-defects report): the ORIGINAL single-event condition (install-touchpoint
AND (credential-scan OR bulk-egress OR hide-artifacts)) could never fire
against the actual attack chain as narrated above -- the skill-install
touchpoint and the post-install payload activity are separate
process-creation events, AND the two selections' own `ParentImage` sets did
not even overlap on the credential-scan branch (`claude.exe`/`cursor.exe`
vs. `node.exe`/`powershell.exe`), making that branch structurally
unreachable regardless of event timing. This rule now expresses the two
stages as a `temporal_ordered` correlation: a Claude Code/Cursor-attributed
skill-install/egress touchpoint, FOLLOWED BY a post-install process either
touching a credential location, bulk-egressing, or hiding its own artifacts,
on the same host within a short window.

Related rules (Nx campaign cluster; a fifth vector, Megalodon, was added
later -- see that rule's note on its sourcing): cross-reference
observed_mini_shai_hulud_npm_supply_chain_c2_t1071.yml (1st vector) +
observed_s1ngularity_nx_npm_token_exfil_t1195_002.yml (2nd vector) +
observed_nx_console_t1195_002.yml (3rd vector) in the same corpus.

Source: first-party Docker engineering blog post (docker.com/blog/
ai-coding-agent-horror-stories-security-risks 2026-05). Aggregated from
1 first-party Docker disclosure (Issue 1 of 5-issue serial roadmap).
falsepositives: Legitimate developer install of a public skill into `.claude/skills/` with broad tool permissions for a personal workflow (review skill provenance + publisher reputation; pin known-safe skill source) -- exclude known-trusted publisher identities

AI coding assistant tutorials / educational content that demonstrate skill install + credential reading (e.g., legitimate `aws sts get-caller-identity` example) -- exclude by tutorial-marker comment in SKILL.md
Build pipeline that legitimately reads `.npmrc` / `GITHUB_TOKEN` as part of CI workflow (exclude by source-host CI runner hostname or session-user svc-account)

The `Computer`-level group-by correlates same-host activity, not same-process-tree activity -- a developer machine running many concurrent, unrelated Claude Code sessions and credential-adjacent tooling could coincidentally satisfy the ordering within the 5-minute window; narrow further with a process-tree/session correlation field if your log source provides one

description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the s1ngularity Nx command-line
supply chain compromise (Docker AI Coding Agent Horror Stories Issue 1 anchor,
May 2026; 1000+ developer tokens exfiltrated). Part of the broader Nx campaign
cluster alongside Mini Shai-Hulud npm, ClawHavoc Claude Skills, and
nx-console VS Code extension. Attack chain:

(1) Compromised Nx CLI installer (npm install -g nx affected version range)
triggers post-install hook with elevated developer-machine privileges.
(2) Credential harvest sweeps known token locations -- ~/.npmrc, GitHub PAT
files, ~/.aws/credentials, environment variables matching NPM_TOKEN /
GITHUB_TOKEN / AWS_ACCESS_KEY patterns.
(3) Bulk exfiltration over HTTPS POST to attacker-controlled endpoints
with batching to avoid single-request size telemetry.
(4) Persistent foothold via modified package-lock.json + worm propagation
to downstream project npm scripts.

Detection logic (CORRELATION, revised 2026-09-04 -- see this corpus's
rule-defects report): the ORIGINAL single-event condition (install AND
(credential-scan OR bulk-egress)) could never fire against the actual
attack chain, since the install step and the post-install child-process
activity are separate process-creation events that never share one log
record. This rule now expresses the two stages as a `temporal_ordered`
correlation: an Nx-family npm install, FOLLOWED BY a post-install process
either touching a known credential-file location or egressing via a
bulk-POST-shaped command, on the same host within a short window.
Cross-references the broader Nx campaign cluster -- correlate hits with
observed_mini_shai_hulud_npm_supply_chain_c2_t1071,
observed_nx_console_t1195_002, and observed_clawhavoc_claude_skills_t1195_002
(this corpus's "Nx campaign" cluster, five vectors total including this
one) for campaign-wide detection coverage.

Context: GitGuardian 2026 report 28.65M secret-leak baseline + AI-commit
token-leak rate 3.2 percent vs human-baseline 1.5 percent (Docker article
quantitative anchor); Docker philosophy explicit "sandboxing structural over
detection" (sbx CLI microVM) -- WRG complementary detection-as-code layer
fills the Docker-acknowledged detection gap. Source: first-party
Docker engineering blog post (docker.com/blog/ai-coding-agent-horror-stories
-security-risks 2026-05).

Aggregated from 1 first-party Docker disclosure (Issue 1 of 5-issue serial
roadmap).
falsepositives: Legitimate Nx CLI install at safe versions for new project bootstrap -- pin version range against Docker disclosure indicators of compromise (IoC) and exclude known-safe versions
Build pipeline that reads .npmrc / GITHUB_TOKEN as part of normal CI workflow -- exclude by source-host identity (CI runner hostname) or session-user (svc account)
Developer-tool egress with curl / Invoke-WebRequest is common in install scripts that fetch supplementary assets -- combine with credential-file scan selection to reduce false positives

The `Computer`-level group-by correlates same-host activity, not same-process-tree activity -- a developer machine running many concurrent, unrelated npm installs and credential-adjacent tooling could coincidentally satisfy the ordering within the 5-minute window; narrow further with a process-tree/session correlation field if your log source provides one
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment

description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the s1ngularity Nx command-line
supply chain compromise (Docker AI Coding Agent Horror Stories Issue 1 anchor,
May 2026; 1000+ developer tokens exfiltrated). Part of the broader Nx campaign
cluster alongside Mini Shai-Hulud npm, ClawHavoc Claude Skills, and
nx-console VS Code extension. Attack chain:

(1) Compromised Nx CLI installer (npm install -g nx affected version range)
triggers post-install hook with elevated developer-machine privileges.
(2) Credential harvest sweeps known token locations -- ~/.npmrc, GitHub PAT
files, ~/.aws/credentials, environment variables matching NPM_TOKEN /
GITHUB_TOKEN / AWS_ACCESS_KEY patterns.
(3) Bulk exfiltration over HTTPS POST to attacker-controlled endpoints
with batching to avoid single-request size telemetry.
(4) Persistent foothold via modified package-lock.json + worm propagation
to downstream project npm scripts.

Detection logic (CORRELATION, revised 2026-09-04 -- see this corpus's
rule-defects report): the ORIGINAL single-event condition (install AND
(credential-scan OR bulk-egress)) could never fire against the actual
attack chain, since the install step and the post-install child-process
activity are separate process-creation events that never share one log
record. This rule now expresses the two stages as a `temporal_ordered`
correlation: an Nx-family npm install, FOLLOWED BY a post-install process
either touching a known credential-file location or egressing via a
bulk-POST-shaped command, on the same host within a short window.
Cross-references the broader Nx campaign cluster -- correlate hits with
observed_mini_shai_hulud_npm_supply_chain_c2_t1071,
observed_nx_console_t1195_002, and observed_clawhavoc_claude_skills_t1195_002
(this corpus's "Nx campaign" cluster, five vectors total including this
one) for campaign-wide detection coverage.

Context: GitGuardian 2026 report 28.65M secret-leak baseline + AI-commit
token-leak rate 3.2 percent vs human-baseline 1.5 percent (Docker article
quantitative anchor); Docker philosophy explicit "sandboxing structural over
detection" (sbx CLI microVM) -- WRG complementary detection-as-code layer
fills the Docker-acknowledged detection gap. Source: first-party
Docker engineering blog post (docker.com/blog/ai-coding-agent-horror-stories
-security-risks 2026-05).

Aggregated from 1 first-party Docker disclosure (Issue 1 of 5-issue serial
roadmap).
falsepositives: Legitimate Nx CLI install at safe versions for new project bootstrap -- pin version range against Docker disclosure indicators of compromise (IoC) and exclude known-safe versions
Build pipeline that reads .npmrc / GITHUB_TOKEN as part of normal CI workflow -- exclude by source-host identity (CI runner hostname) or session-user (svc account)
Developer-tool egress with curl / Invoke-WebRequest is common in install scripts that fetch supplementary assets -- combine with credential-file scan selection to reduce false positives

The `Computer`-level group-by correlates same-host activity, not same-process-tree activity -- a developer machine running many concurrent, unrelated npm installs and credential-adjacent tooling could coincidentally satisfy the ordering within the 5-minute window; narrow further with a process-tree/session correlation field if your log source provides one
